sentences.text: Adult Hongshanornis longicresta measured roughly 320 millimeters across its wings and weighed about 50 grams, similar in size to a modern thrush.
Scientists identified a distinct bone at the jaw's tip that they likened to the predentary bone seen in ornithischian dinosaurs.
Among its feet, the third toe was notably longer than the others.
The total surface area covered by its wings amounted to 0.016 square meters.
This bird possessed at least ten tail feathers, a count exceeding that of other early fan-tailed birds.
While the original description proposed a large feathered crest, a second specimen showed shorter feathers near the snout, suggesting the first might be a preservation artifact.
The holotype specimen was recovered in 2005 and is currently kept at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing.
Gizzard stones found inside one individual imply that this animal ate plants.
The lack of slots in the wings indicates the bird likely flew at relatively high speeds.
It probably flapped its wings continuously when moving slowly but switched to bounding flight at higher speeds.
This species serves as the namesake for the family Hongshanornithidae.
Hongshanornis is an ornithuromorph bird known from early Cretaceous lake deposits in the Yixian Formation of Inner Mongolia, China.
The time range for this genus spans from the Barremian to the Aptian, between 125.77 and 119.57 million years ago.
It is debated whether Hongshanornis possessed a beak, as some scientists argue its jaw bone lacks the characteristic pits and grooves found in early beaked birds.
